summary: Watermelon radish and watercress salad: thinly sliced watermelon radish arranged in a circle on chilled plates, topped with a tall mound of lightly dressed watercress, fresh figs, pomegranate arils, Parmigiano shavings and toasted walnuts; serves 4 in 10 minutes.
glance: 1 large watermelon radish, sliced very thinly (a mandoline helps)
2 fig halves, 1 tablespoon pomegranate arils, 4 cheese shavings, 3 walnut halves
faq: What is a watermelon radish?
Green on the outside, but when sliced intensely red in the middle, looking like tiny watermelons. Slice it thinly and evenly; a mandoline is excellent for that.
What watercress should I buy?

Hydroponic watercress with the root ball intact is available year-round at specialty markets. Look for bright, fresh leaves with no signs of wilt. The tart, peppery cress is a great foil for the sweet figs and pomegranate.
How do I make the salad look nice?

Aim to make a tall, high mound of the dressed watercress in the center of each plate and don't let it spread out; that's the critical step. Arrange the radish slices in a circle on chilled plates first.
How is the watercress dressed?
Toss with a bit of olive oil and a squeeze of lemon juice just before plating.
What other watermelon dish is there?
The author suggests his seared watermelon, "not the same melon, but fun."

summary: Fromage forte ("strong cheese") from a Jacques Pepin cookbook: 1/2 pound of odds and ends of good cheese processed with dry white wine, garlic and black pepper until creamy, with yogurt if needed; makes about 2 cups for crostini or dip and improves over a couple of days.
glance: about 2 cups, for crostini topping or dip
1/2 pound cheese scraps, 1/2 cup dry white wine, 1 clove garlic, black pepper
in the refrigerator; flavor improves over a couple of days
faq: What is fromage forte?
"Strong cheese": the author's best way to use up all the odds and ends of good cheese in your refrigerator, learned from a Jacques Pepin cookbook. It's sometimes spelled fromage fort.
What cheeses should I use?
Just about any mixture of quality cheeses, but not "grocery store" cheddar-type products. The author likes a mix of strong, mild, hard, creamy and blue cheeses to maximize flavor.
How do I make it?

Trim any rock-hard or moldy parts off the cheese, then spin the cheese, wine, pepper and garlic in a food processor for a few minutes until no large chunks remain and it's fairly smooth. If needed, add more wine or yogurt, and salt.
How thick should it be?
Thick enough to stand up; you don't want it runny. If too thick and you don't want more wine, use a little yogurt.
How do I serve it?
On simple crostini of baguette slices brushed with olive oil and toasted briefly under the broiler, either as is or run back under the broiler to brown the cheese.

summary: Caramelized apple and blue cheese crostini from the Herbivoracious cookbook: baguette slices brushed with tarragon oil and toasted about 5 minutes at 400°F, topped with apple wedges browned about 5 minutes in butter, blue cheese, crushed and whole tarragon and flaky salt; makes 16 in 20 minutes.
glance: 2 small crisp cooking apples such as Pink Lady, 16 wedges, deeply caramelized
1/4 cup creamy blue, such as Blue de Causses or Gorgonzola dolce
faq: What is the key to these crostini?
Use a good, crisp cooking apple and really caramelize it deeply. A quickly made tarragon oil and fresh tarragon leaves together amp up the flavor.
What blue cheese works best?
A creamy blue that gets a little melty on the warm apples, such as Blue de Causses, though any blue cheese will work.
Can I use another herb?
Instead of tarragon you could use basil or even arugula.
How do I make the tarragon oil?

Roughly puree about 1/2 cup of tarragon leaves (setting aside 32 nice ones) with 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a mortar and pestle or mini processor, brush the baguette slices with it, and save the crushed tarragon for garnish.
How should I serve them?
With a crisp, dry white wine as an elegant pre-dinner snack. A few grains of fancy finishing salt, such as red Hawaiian salt, add crunch and interest.

summary: Summery risotto with corn, zucchini and cherry tomato oil: arborio cooked with white wine and mild broth (simmered with the corn cobs) added a ladle at a time, finished with fresh corn, diced zucchini and Parmigiano and dressed with a tomato olive oil; serves 6.
glance: 2 cups arborio or carnaroli; check a grain every minute after 16 minutes
6 cups mildly flavored vegetable broth, simmered with the corn cobs
6 tablespoons olive oil pureed with cherry tomatoes and salt; keep leftovers only a few days
Vegetarian and gluten-free; vegan if you omit the cheese
faq: Why use mild broth for risotto?
The broth is greatly reduced and concentrated in cooking, so a strong broth would be overpowering when finished. Here the corn cobs are added to the simmering broth to bring up the corn flavor.
Do I have to stir risotto continuously?
No. Add the broth one ladle at a time, stirring very frequently; continuously isn't necessary. When the rice begins to dry out add another ladle.
When do I add the vegetables?

After about 16 minutes, begin to check a grain every minute; when there is a slight white pinhead that is a bit tough inside, add the corn and zucchini. Within 3-10 minutes the rice should be tender with a hint of toothsomeness, surrounded by creamy, starchy goodness.
What is the cherry tomato oil?

Olive oil pureed with raw cherry tomatoes and salt and steeped half an hour if possible, then strained. The water emulsifies the oil, so it's more like a tomato dressing, with lots of flavor and ready in 2 minutes. For a more concentrated oil, oven-dry the tomatoes first.
How long can I keep the oil?
Only a few days: there's a risk of anaerobic bacteria in home-flavored oils. Refrigerate if not using soon.

summary: Spectacular chocolate-espresso brownies, a dense, moist, cakey brownie adapted from Ina Garten: melted butter and chocolate beaten with eggs, instant espresso and sugar, folded with flour, half the chocolate chips sprinkled on top, baked at 350°F for 25-30 minutes in a 13x9 pan; makes 10 large or 18 medium.
glance: 350°F: 20 minutes, rap the pan, then 5-10 more until a toothpick comes out clean
12 ounces semi-sweet chips (half melted, half on top) plus 4 ounces unsweetened
13 x 9 inches, at least 1 inch deep
faq: Cakey or fudgy?

The author likes a cakey brownie, but one that has to be very moist and dense cake. The recipe has a long lineage: from Ina Garten, who adapted it from the Soho Charcuterie Cookbook by Francine Scherer and Madeline Poley (1983).
What did the author change?

He omits the walnuts, doubles the salt, upgrades the chocolate, simplifies the steps to use one fewer bowl, and sprinkles half of the chocolate chips over the top of the batter instead of mixing them in, giving creamy-chocolate rivers on the surface.
Why instant espresso?
He uses instant espresso instead of instant coffee, such as Medaglia D'Oro, or two packets of Starbucks VIA instant coffee (decaf or regular); it tastes great in baked goods.
How do I avoid overbaking?
Bake 20 minutes, give the pan a rap to force out bubbles, then bake 5-10 more minutes until a toothpick comes out clean. Don't overbake. Cool slightly before serving.
How do I add the chocolate to the eggs?
Cool the melted butter and chocolate at least 5 minutes, then drizzle it in slowly so you don't cook the eggs.

summary: Most spectacular chocolate and coffee brownies, adapted from Ina Garten's Outrageous Brownies (halved for a 12x9 pan): melted butter and chocolate beaten with eggs, instant espresso and sugar, folded with flour, chip-topped and baked at 350°F; makes at least 10 large or 18 moderate brownies.
glance: at least 10 large or 18 more moderate brownies
12 x 9 inches, at least 1 inch deep
350°F: 20 minutes, rap the pan, then more until done
dense, moist cakey; use cake flour for lighter and cakier
Vegetarian; not vegan or gluten-free; nut-free
yield: at least 10 large or 18 moderate brownies
faq: Where does the recipe come from?

The author found it in Ina Garten's Outrageous Brownies, which she got from William Morrow's SoHo Charcuterie Cookbook. He halved it from a 12x18 pan to 12x9, omitted the walnuts (his is a nut-allergy family), doubled the salt, upgraded the chocolate, used one less bowl and used instant espresso.
What kind of brownie is it?
The author likes a cakey brownie that is very moist and dense, with a seriously chocolaty punch; everyone he's fed them to agrees. He says he doesn't think he'll try a different recipe again.
Can I make them lighter?
If you want them really light and cakey, use cake flour instead of all-purpose. The author found it changed the texture dramatically, though he prefers them denser.
Why put chips on top?
Sprinkling half of the chocolate chips over the batter instead of mixing them in gives incredible creamy-chocolate rivers on the surface.
What instant coffee should I use?
Instant espresso such as Medaglia D'Oro, or Starbucks Via packets. The author doesn't drink it anymore but says it tastes great in baked goods.

summary: A review of The Newlywed Kitchen by Lorna Yee and Ali Basye, with the authors' zucchini fritters recipe reprinted with permission: grated zucchini salted and squeezed, mixed with garlic, egg, Parmesan and flour and fried 3 minutes then 2-3 minutes in olive oil, with a lemon-parsley yogurt sauce; makes 10.
glance: The Newlywed Kitchen: Delicious Meals for Couples Cooking Together by Lorna Yee and Ali Basye
about 3 minutes, flip, then 2-3 more minutes, in 3 tablespoons olive oil
3/4 cup Greek yogurt, lemon juice, parsley
faq: What is The Newlywed Kitchen?

A beautiful, charming cookbook for couples just starting out in marriage, exploring cooking together, with recipes and endearing stories from a wide range of culinary professionals about cooking with their beloved in the first years of marriage. The author says to give it as a shower gift.
How do I keep zucchini fritters from being soggy?
Combine the grated zucchini and salt in a sieve over a bowl and squeeze the water out with your hands (you should be able to remove about 1/2 cup).
How do I fry them?

Spoon heaping tablespoons of batter into hot olive oil over medium-high heat without letting them touch, brown about 3 minutes, lifting the edge to check the color, then flip and cook another 2 to 3 minutes.
How should I serve them?
Fresh out of the frying pan for maximum crispy goodness, with the tangy yogurt sauce.
Whose recipe is it?
Lorna Yee and Ali Basye's, reprinted with permission; the author loves any little crispy pan-fried fritter.

summary: Roasted purple cauliflower with sherry vinaigrette and fried capers: four heads of cauliflower roasted at 400°F until tender with caramelized brown spots, tossed with piquillo peppers, dark-fried capers and a sherry-lemon-garlic vinaigrette, topped with garlic breadcrumbs and broiled; serves 8 in 45 minutes.
glance: 400°F until quite tender with significant brown spots
2/3 cup olive oil, 1/4 cup sherry vinegar, lemon juice, garlic
faq: How do I roast cauliflower?

Break it into large bite-sized florets, toss with olive oil and salt, and roast at 400°F (convection if you have it) in two pans, tossing occasionally, until quite tender with significant brown spots. You don't get the real roasted flavor until you see those caramelized bits. They shrink a lot.
How do I fry capers?
Rinse and dry them, then carefully fry in canola oil, watching out for spattering, until quite dark but not burned, and drain on paper towel.
Does purple cauliflower keep its color?
The author says the purple cauliflower really retained its color when roasted.
How do I dress it?

Let the cauliflower cool a few minutes, add the capers and red peppers, and toss with the vinaigrette a little at a time until highly flavored but not drenched. Top with breadcrumbs tossed with olive oil and garlic, broil until toasty, and garnish with lots of flat parsley.
Why this combination?
The author wanted a quick potluck dish with Spanish flavors in his mind: capers (inspired by the fried capers in the Cafe Flora Caesar salad) and a sherry vinaigrette.

summary: Ultra-local homefries with tomatoes and eggs: 1.5 pounds of skin-on diced potatoes fried in a single layer in a big cast-iron skillet, flipped every 3 minutes until deep golden brown and crispy, with onion and chili, served with sliced tomatoes and sunny-side-up eggs; serves 2.
glance: 2 as a major part of a meal
single layer, flipped every 3 minutes, until deep golden brown
Vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free (not vegan with eggs)
yield: 2 as a major part of a meal
faq: How do I get crispy homefries?

Use your biggest skillet, preferably cast iron, to maximize surface area. Fry the potato in a single layer (or as close as possible), flipping every 3 minutes or so with a spatula and getting uncooked surfaces onto the skillet, until deep golden brown. Serve while still hot and crispy.
Why are restaurant homefries often soggy?
They're usually cut too large and cooked in a big pile on a flat-top griddle, where they mostly steam.
How do I cut the potatoes?
Into 3/8-inch dice with the skin on; any kind of potato works.
How should I serve them?
Topped with a fried egg (sunny-side up, so the yolk mixes with the potatoes and tomato juices) and slices of garden tomato, finished with flaky sea salt and fresh ground pepper.
What does ultra-local mean here?

Everything but the salt and olive oil was local: purple Viking potatoes and Cherokee tomatoes from the backyard, chili de arbol from Alvarez farm, onions from the farmer's market, and eggs from a friend's backyard chickens.

summary: Crostini with truffled cheese, lentils du Puy and apple: garlicky lentils simmered until tender but intact and cooled, spooned onto oiled, toasted bread topped with melted semi-soft truffled sheep's milk cheese, with diced apple and microgreens; makes 8, and the lentils can be made the day before.
glance: 1 cup lentils du Puy with 2 cups water, simmered until tender but not falling apart
8 slices semi-soft truffled sheep's milk cheese, melted on the toast
lentils the day before; warm to serve
faq: What cheese should I use?
A truffled cheese: look for a semi-soft sheep's milk one that will melt well; a good cheesemonger usually has one or two.
What lentils work?
Lentils du Puy or black lentils, both of which hold their shape when tender. Plain brown lentils won't work as well.
What texture should the lentils have?
Crucial to making this delicious: neither dry and mealy nor unpleasantly wet. Stirring in a little more fruity olive oil at the last minute is a big help.
Can I make it ahead?
Yes: prepare the lentils the day before and just warm them up when you're ready to serve.
What does the apple do?
Finely diced apple gives a sweet, fresh counterpoint to the earthy flavors of the truffle and lentils.
What bread should I use?
Small slices of crusty bread brushed generously with olive oil on both sides and toasted. Don't pile the lentils so high that it's hard to eat.
